title: Chemical Energetics
seo_title: Secondary 4 Chemistry: Chemical Energetics Worksheets (O-Level 6092 with Answers)
standard_text: Describe the meaning of exothermic and endothermic reactions and represent them by energy profile diagrams; state that ΔH is negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions; describe activation energy and show it on energy profile diagrams; describe bond breaking as endothermic and bond making as exothermic and explain the enthalpy change of a reaction in these terms; calculate enthalpy changes from bond energies (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 4 O-Level Chemistry worksheets on chemical energetics: exothermic and endothermic reactions, ΔH, energy profile diagrams, activation energy and bond energy calculations. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Exothermic: ΔH negative. Endothermic: ΔH positive.
key_sub: ΔH = energy to break bonds − energy from making bonds.
body_html:
How to think about it

Reactions give out or take in energy.

  • Exothermic: energy given out, temperature rises, products lower in energy, ΔH negative. Endothermic: the opposite.
  • Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react; a catalyst lowers it but does not change ΔH.
  • Breaking bonds takes in energy; making bonds gives out energy. ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds made).
Example

H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. ΔH?

broken: 436 + 242 = 678

made: 2 × 431 = 862

678 − 862

Answer: −184 kJ/mol

Example

Temperature falls from 25.0 °C to 19.5 °C. Type?

energy taken in

Answer: endothermic

Common mistakes

  • Saying bond breaking releases energy.
  • Giving an exothermic reaction a positive ΔH.
  • Calculating ΔH as bonds made − bonds broken (the sign comes out wrong).
  • Thinking a catalyst changes ΔH.

faq.q: How do you calculate ΔH from bond energies?
faq.a: Add up the energies of all the bonds broken in the reactants, add up the energies of all the bonds made in the products, then ΔH = bonds broken − bonds made.

faq.q: How do you read an energy profile diagram?
faq.a: If the products are lower than the reactants the reaction is exothermic; if higher, endothermic. The hump from the reactants to the peak is the activation energy.

faq.q: Why do exothermic reactions need activation energy?
faq.a: Bonds in the reactants must start to break before new bonds can form, and this needs a minimum amount of energy.
